figures.teaches: A systematic fistula examination localizes dysfunction before thrombosis.
figures.content: Center: realistic line drawing of a left forearm radiocephalic fistula with the anastomosis at the wrist, needling segment and outflow vein up the arm to the shoulder and chest. Six numbered steps around it: 1 'Look' (swelling, chest collaterals, aneurysm, thin shiny skin); 2 'Feel' (continuous thrill normal; pulsatile = outflow narrowing; flat = inflow problem); 3 'Raise the arm' (should collapse; stays full = outflow stenosis); 4 'Augment' (occlude above anastomosis; pulse should strengthen; weak = inflow stenosis); 5 'Listen' (continuous low-pitched bruit normal; high-pitched or systolic only = narrowing); 6 'Check the hand' (color, warmth, refill, sensation; cold painful hand = steal). Bottom strip: 'Exam vs angiography (142 fistulas): outflow sensitivity 92%, specificity 86%; inflow 85%, 71%'. Footer '© renalcarematters.com'.

figures.teaches: Access planning is a sequence across years tied to the ESKD Life-Plan.
figures.content: Horizontal timeline. Left: 'CKD clinic, eGFR under 30: Life-Plan conversation; protect arm veins; no PICC'. Next: 'eGFR 15-20: refer for access assessment (KDOQI 2019, expert opinion); vessel mapping if high risk of failure'. Next: 'Fistula created: maturation check by 4-6 weeks'. Next: 'Dialysis start with mature access'. Branches above the line: 'Peritoneal dialysis catheter: both arms preserved'; 'Living donor transplant expected: catheter or PD may bridge'. Branch below: 'Emergency start: tunneled catheter = bridge with an end date; permanent access planned at once'. Final box: 'Annual Life-Plan review (expert opinion)'. Small icon of the access sequence: forearm first, then upper arm, then graft. Footer '© renalcarematters.com'.
